prompt: Expected number of coin flips to get the first head (fair coin). Set up the recurrence, do not just recall the number.
reveal: Let E be the answer. One flip always happens. With probability 1/2 it is a head and you stop; with probability 1/2 it is a tail and you are back where you started. So E = 1 + (1/2)(0) + (1/2)(E), giving E/2 = 1, so E = 2. The general result for probability p is 1/p — a geometric distribution.

prompt: A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000. You test positive. Roughly what is the probability you have it, and what drives the answer?
reveal: Roughly 1%. Out of 1,000,000 people: ~100 have it and ~99 test positive; ~999,900 do not and ~1% — about 9,999 — test positive falsely. So P(disease | positive) ≈ 99 / (99 + 9999) ≈ 1%. The driver is the base rate: when the prior is tiny, false positives from the huge healthy population swamp true positives. This is base-rate neglect.

prompt: State linearity of expectation and why it is unusually powerful. Use it on: expected number of fixed points in a random permutation of n items.
reveal: E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] regardless of whether X and Y are independent — that independence-freedom is what makes it powerful. For fixed points, define an indicator Xᵢ = 1 if item i maps to position i. P(Xᵢ=1) = 1/n, so E[Xᵢ] = 1/n. Summing over n items: E[X] = n · (1/n) = 1. Exactly one fixed point on average, for any n — and the indicators are dependent, which does not matter.

prompt: Define variance and standard deviation, and state why standard deviation is usually reported instead.
reveal: Variance is E[(X − μ)²], the mean squared deviation from the mean; equivalently E[X²] − (E[X])². Standard deviation is its square root. Standard deviation is reported because squaring changes the units (dollars become dollars-squared); the square root restores the original units, so it is directly comparable to the data.

prompt: State the central limit theorem precisely and name one common way people misapply it.
reveal: The CLT says the distribution of the SAMPLE MEAN of n independent, identically distributed variables with finite variance approaches a normal distribution as n grows — regardless of the original distribution’s shape. Common misapplication: assuming the DATA itself becomes normal (it does not — only the sampling distribution of the mean does), or applying it to heavy-tailed distributions with infinite variance, where it fails.

prompt: Monty Hall: you pick door 1, the host opens door 3 revealing a goat, and offers a switch. Switch or stay? Justify without hand-waving.
reveal: Switch — it wins 2/3 of the time. Your initial pick is right with probability 1/3, so the prize is behind one of the other two doors with probability 2/3. The host, who knows the layout and always opens a goat door, concentrates that entire 2/3 onto the single remaining door. The key premise is that the host’s choice is not random — if he opened a door at random and it happened to show a goat, switching would be 50/50.

prompt: What defines a Markov chain, and what does a stationary distribution mean? Give the gambler’s-ruin intuition.
reveal: A Markov chain is a state process where the next state depends only on the current state, not the history — the memoryless property. A stationary distribution π satisfies πP = π: once the chain is distributed as π, it stays that way. Gambler’s ruin: a random walk between 0 and N with absorbing barriers — with a fair coin, the probability of hitting N before 0 starting from k is k/N, and the game ends with probability 1. Against a house with an edge, ruin becomes near-certain over enough plays.

prompt: Expected number of flips to see two consecutive heads. Set up the states and solve.
reveal: Define states by progress: S0 = no useful streak, S1 = one head so far. From S0: one flip, then half the time you reach S1, half you stay in S0 — E0 = 1 + ½E1 + ½E0. From S1: one flip, half the time you are done, half you fall back to S0 — E1 = 1 + ½(0) + ½E0. Substituting gives E0 = 6. The general pattern for k consecutive heads with a fair coin is 2^(k+1) − 2, so k=1 gives 2 and k=2 gives 6.

prompt: Coupon collector: how many draws to collect all n distinct coupons? Derive it with linearity.
reveal: Break the process into phases: phase i is the time to get the i-th NEW coupon after having i−1. In that phase the chance any draw is new is (n−i+1)/n, so the expected wait is a geometric with mean n/(n−i+1). By linearity, total = n(1/n + 1/(n−1) + ... + 1/1) = n·Hₓ ≈ n ln n + 0.577n. So collecting all 50 states takes roughly 225 draws, not 50 — the last few coupons dominate the cost.

prompt: Expected maximum of n independent fair dice rolls. What is the trick that avoids brute force?
reveal: Use the tail-sum formula: for a non-negative integer variable, E[X] = Σ P(X ≥ k). P(max ≥ k) = 1 − P(all rolls < k) = 1 − ((k−1)/6)^n. So E[max] = Σ from k=1 to 6 of [1 − ((k−1)/6)^n]. For n=2 this gives 161/36 ≈ 4.47. The trick is that P(max ≤ k) factorizes into independent per-roll probabilities, whereas the density of the max does not — always attack max/min problems through the CDF.

prompt: Distinguish mutually exclusive from independent events. Can two events with positive probability be both?
reveal: Mutually exclusive means they cannot co-occur: P(A∩B) = 0. Independent means one gives no information about the other: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). No — if both have positive probability they cannot be both, because exclusivity forces P(A∩B)=0 while independence would require P(A)P(B) > 0. In fact mutually exclusive events are maximally DEPENDENT: knowing A occurred tells you B definitely did not.

prompt: The birthday problem: why does it only take 23 people for a 50% chance, and what is the general heuristic?
reveal: Count the PAIRS, not the people: 23 people form C(23,2) = 253 pairs, each with a 1/365 chance of matching. Compute via the complement: P(all distinct) = (365/365)(364/365)...(343/365) ≈ 0.493, so a match has probability ≈ 0.507. The general heuristic: with N equally likely values you need roughly √N samples for a 50% collision chance — which is exactly the birthday bound behind hash-collision attacks and why a 64-bit hash starts colliding around 2³² items.

prompt: What is maximum likelihood estimation, and what does it give for the mean of a normal sample?
reveal: MLE picks the parameter value that makes the OBSERVED data most probable: maximize the likelihood ∏ f(xᵢ; θ), usually by maximizing the log-likelihood since sums are easier to differentiate. For a normal with unknown mean μ, the log-likelihood is −Σ(xᵢ−μ)²/(2σ²) plus constants; differentiating and setting to zero gives μ̂ = sample mean. Note the MLE for the VARIANCE divides by n and is biased; the unbiased estimator divides by n−1 — a standard interview follow-up.

prompt: Derive the closed form for ordinary least squares and state what each part means geometrically.
reveal: Minimize ‖y − Xβ‖². Expand: βᵀXᵀXβ − 2βᵀXᵀy + yᵀy. Differentiate with respect to β and set to zero: 2XᵀXβ − 2Xᵀy = 0, giving the normal equations XᵀXβ = Xᵀy and β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. Geometrically, Xβ̂ is the ORTHOGONAL PROJECTION of y onto the column space of X — the residual y − Xβ̂ is perpendicular to every column of X, which is exactly what Xᵀ(y − Xβ̂) = 0 says. XᵀX is invertible only if the columns are linearly independent, i.e. no perfect multicollinearity.

prompt: What does ridge regression change in the OLS solution, and why does it help with multicollinearity?
reveal: Ridge minimizes ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖², giving β̂ = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy — the only change is adding λ to the diagonal. That guarantees invertibility even when XᵀX is singular or near-singular, which is precisely the multicollinearity case: correlated columns make XᵀX nearly singular, so its inverse has huge entries and coefficient variance explodes. Adding λI bounds the smallest eigenvalue away from zero, shrinking coefficients and trading a little bias for a large variance reduction.

prompt: Lasso versus ridge: which produces sparsity, and what is the geometric reason?
reveal: Lasso (L1 penalty) produces sparsity — it drives coefficients exactly to zero, performing feature selection; ridge (L2) shrinks them toward zero but never to zero. The geometric reason: the L1 constraint region is a diamond with CORNERS on the axes, and the elliptical contours of the squared-error loss are most likely to first touch the region at a corner — where some coordinates are exactly zero. The L2 region is a smooth circle with no corners, so the contact point generically has all coordinates non-zero. Lasso also has no closed form, requiring coordinate descent or LARS.

prompt: State the bias-variance decomposition and explain why a more complex model is not always better.
reveal: Expected test error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias is error from wrong assumptions (a model too simple to capture the structure); variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample (a model so flexible it fits noise). Increasing complexity lowers bias but raises variance, so total error is U-shaped — there is an optimum, and pushing past it overfits. Irreducible noise sets the floor no model can beat. Regularization, more data, and ensembling are the standard variance-reduction levers.

prompt: Pearson versus Spearman correlation: when is each appropriate, and what does correlation fail to capture?
reveal: Pearson measures LINEAR association and assumes roughly interval data; it is sensitive to outliers and to non-linear but monotone relationships. Spearman is Pearson applied to the RANKS, so it captures any monotone relationship and is robust to outliers and skew — preferred for financial returns and heavy-tailed data. Both fail on non-monotone dependence: y = x² over a symmetric range has essentially zero correlation despite perfect determinism. Correlation also says nothing about causation or about tail dependence.

prompt: What does a p-value actually mean, and name two common misinterpretations.
reveal: A p-value is P(observing data at least this extreme | the null hypothesis is TRUE). Misinterpretation 1: treating it as the probability the null is true — that is a Bayesian posterior and requires a prior. Misinterpretation 2: treating p < 0.05 as proof of a large or important effect — with enough data, a trivially small effect becomes significant, so effect size and confidence intervals matter more. A third trap is p-hacking: testing many hypotheses and reporting the significant ones without correcting for multiplicity.

prompt: How does Monte Carlo estimation work, and how does its error scale with sample size?
reveal: Estimate an expectation by drawing n independent samples and averaging: μ̂ = (1/n)Σf(Xᵢ). By the law of large numbers it converges to the true value, and by the CLT the standard error is σ/√n — so accuracy improves only as the SQUARE ROOT of effort: 100× more samples for 10× more precision. Crucially that rate is independent of DIMENSION, which is why Monte Carlo beats grid-based numerical integration in high dimensions. Variance-reduction techniques (antithetic variates, control variates, importance sampling) buy accuracy without more samples.
